question: What is the main way we define gender-based violence (GBV)?

options.A: Harmful acts based on sex or gender identity
options.B: Violent crimes committed exclusively against adult males
options.C: Accidental domestic injuries occurring at home
options.D: Physical injuries sustained during a street fight

explanation: GBV happens because of a person's sex or gender roles, rather than just random bad luck or street crime. You've got this! [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h1)

question: Why are nurses often the very first people to spot victims of gender-based violence?

options.A: Patients often disclose abuse first to trusted frontline healthcare workers
options.B: Medical staff are legally required to investigate crime scenes directly
options.C: Hospitals are the only safe havens available for survivors
options.D: Nurses have direct legal authority to arrest suspected perpetrators

explanation: Because you offer a kind and confidential ear, patients feel safe enough to open up to you during routine checks. Great nursing instinct! [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h1)

question: Which type of abuse involves controlling money and financial resources to keep power over a partner?
explanation: Economic abuse traps people by cutting them off from money, jobs, and financial freedom. Spotting this helps us understand the full picture of abuse. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h2)

question: A patient walks into your clinic with constant headaches, tummy pain, and worry, but tests show nothing physically wrong. What should you keep in mind?

options.D: Acute food poisoning from expired food

explanation: When physical wounds heal or aren't there, survivors often show stress through ongoing body pains and anxiety. Always look a bit deeper! [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h2)

question: Why must a nurse keep a strict 'chain of custody' when handling forensic evidence?

options.A: To ensure the collected evidence is legally admissible in court
options.B: To reduce hospital supply and inventory costs
options.C: To diagnose underlying sexually transmitted infections faster
options.D: To speed up the patient's physical recovery process

explanation: Keeping strict track of who handles evidence stops it from getting lost or tampered with so it can actually help get justice in court. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h3)

question: How should you write down a patient's story of how an injury happened in their chart?

options.A: Omitting the patient's story to save clinical documentation time
options.B: Writing down personal assumptions about the perpetrator
options.C: Using the patient's exact words in quotation marks
options.D: Summarizing the event using clinical diagnostic slang

explanation: Always use their exact words in quotes! It keeps your notes honest, clear, and legally solid. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h3)

question: Within how many hours of a possible HIV exposure should Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) be started for the best results?
explanation: Time matters! Starting PEP within 72 hours gives the best chance of preventing HIV after an exposure. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h4)

question: An injured survivor of an assault arrives at your facility. What is your very first clinical priority?

options.C: Collecting forensic swabs and clothing fibers

explanation: Saving a life and stabilizing the patient always comes first before collecting evidence or paperwork. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h4)

question: What is the main mindset shift behind trauma-informed care?

options.A: Asking what happened to the patient instead of what is wrong with them
options.B: Minimizing emotional expressions to maintain clinical efficiency
options.C: Determining the legal guilt of the alleged perpetrator immediately
options.D: Focusing exclusively on surgical repair of physical wounds

explanation: Instead of judging a patient's behavior, trauma-informed care reminds us to ask, 'What happened to you?' It's all about empathy. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h5)

question: Why shouldn't you force a survivor to tell every single detail of their assault right away?

options.A: Forced retelling can trigger severe anxiety and re-traumatize the patient
options.B: Police investigations are always hindered by early patient statements
options.C: Medical records do not need any details about the assault
options.D: Physical examination results become invalid if the patient speaks

explanation: Let survivors take their time. Pressing them to talk too soon can overwhelm them and bring back the trauma. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h5)

question: Which Nigerian law provides major legal protection against domestic violence and harmful practices?

options.A: Standard Nursing and Midwifery Council Decree
options.C: Public Health Sanitation and Hygiene Code

explanation: The VAPP Act is a key law in Nigeria meant to protect people from violence at home and in public. Good to know for your exams and practice! [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h6)

question: When does a nurse usually face a tough ethical choice about keeping a patient's secret in GBV cases?

options.A: When scheduling a follow-up clinic appointment for the patient
options.B: When the patient requests standard pain relief medications
options.C: When mandatory reporting laws require disclosing abuse to authorities
options.D: When documenting routine vital signs on a bedside chart

explanation: Balancing your promise of patient privacy with the legal duty to report certain cases can be tricky, but it's a vital nursing skill. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h6)

question: What is the main goal of having a multi-sectoral referral network for GBV survivors?

options.A: To provide comprehensive medical, legal, and social support through coordinated agencies
options.B: To reduce the total number of follow-up medical visits required
options.C: To transfer all administrative responsibilities away from the hospital
options.D: To ensure the police handle every aspect of the patient's recovery

explanation: Healing takes a village! Teamwork between health workers, legal aid, and social services gives survivors the best all-round support. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h7)

question: Your patient is medically ready to leave the clinic, but is terrified to go back to an unsafe home. What should you do?

options.A: Advise the patient to ignore the fear and return home immediately
options.B: Connect the patient with safe shelter and social welfare referral services
options.C: Contact law enforcement to arrest the patient for missing work
options.D: Discharge the patient without discussing housing or safety plans

explanation: Never send a vulnerable patient back into danger. Connecting them with safe housing and social workers is a lifesaver. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T13#GNS312_U4_T13_h7)
